records.bodyText:
Interesting post from Pat Murray.
The Times published an article on the cost of curtailing wind power, their third article on the topic in the past few months, based on data from Octopus Energy.
The headline numbers are indeed large; £1.5B year-to-date, and rising.
But the headline is misleading; £1.28B of that £1.5B, or about 85%, has gone to paying gas turbines near cities to turn on, instead of paying wind turbines to turn off.
Constraint costs should be minimised, all else equal, but there's quite a bit under the hood. Let's break it down.
The economics of wind
Wind and solar economics differ meaningfully from carbon power in 2 important ways:
No marginal cost: the cost of a wind and solar farm is nearly all upfront; the marginal cost of producing an additional unit of power is effectively zero
High covariance: within a (European- sized) country, the amount of solar or wind across the country goes up and down in unison
Together, this means that the more renewables we have, the more likely it is that we produce too much energy at a given time.
Is this a problem?
Not necessarily. If it's cheap enough to build wind and solar farms, you could imagine a lowest-cost energy system driven by overbuilt renewables, where a wind farm operating at a low capacity factor is still more cost-efficient than alternatives like firing up a gas power plant.
This is what we're starting to see in continental Europe; increased solar curtailment, where total generation at times exceeds total demand.
The UK situation is a bit different. Here, much of the wind generation is in Scotland, but most of the demand is in England. And the transmission capacity to bring that Scottish wind to English consumers is constrained, because generation has grown faster than network capacity. (Separating generation from transmission expansion was a deliberate policy decision, and likely the right one historically).
The obvious solution is to build more cables to increase that capacity. And hey, the UK is doing so; the Eastern Green Links are a series of 4 transmission lines from Scotland to England, coming online from 2029-2034, which should more than double the capacity across this constraint.
These cost a pretty penny, about £13B in total. They're all offshore, which costs ~5x the on-land equivalent, but reduces community objections, permitting delays, and the like. Ofgem's analysis suggests they're good value-for-money.
We can also soak up the excess wind in Scotland (through batteries, EVs, industrial processes, etc.) and reduce demand in England when there isn't much cheap generation available. This is part of what flexibility companies like Axle do.
So what's the big deal?
Unsurprisingly for energy, this is a small fight within a larger battle.
Great Britain has one national market for wholesale electricity; that means that a MWh generated in northern Scotland gets paid the same as one generated in London. The wind curtailment issue highlights a shortcoming of that approach: wind developers want to build wherever it's windiest, so it's up to the central planners to approve & plan for the generation and transmission that's in the best interest of the system.
An alternative is locational pricing; different prices in different parts of the country, which create a price signal to, say, build more generation close to consumer.
Economists love this, but most others don't; it creates winners and losers, and would be a very large and disruptive (read: expensive) change to the structure of the energy market.
Last year, the government considered locational pricing, which opened up a pitched battle within industry. The government ruled against it.
Supporters are using wind curtailment to continue fighting this battle, and in the process providing (misleading) ammunition for the 'net zero is bad' crowd.
As always, the truth hides beyond the headlines.

Liverpool Bay is now home to the world’s first offshore platform dedicated to carbon capture and storage and will service a controversial multi-billion pound carbon capture project. 
This will enable CO2 emissions captured as part of the multi-billion pound HyNet project to be  stored indefinitely in rock in depleted gas fields in the Irish Sea.
This platform was delivered in less than 18 months from contract award following an accelerated programme integrating engineering, procurement, construction, and commissioning.
Called Douglas CCS, it comprises 1,885-tonne topside facilities, a supporting jacket structure weighing 1,755 tonnes and eight foundation piles with a combined weight of 730 tonnes, which secure the structure to the seabed.
HyNet, which comprises a consortium of businesses, will produce hydrogen for industrial use by burning natural gas at a facility being built at the Stanlow oil refinery in Ellesmere Port.
Instead of being released into the atmosphere, the CO2 produced by the gas will be captured and sent to Liverpool Bay via a pipeline through North Wales. It is being backed by billions of pounds of Government cash and will likely be operational in 2028.
Carbon capture and storage (CCS) is a controversial method and some experts doubt it is achievable to the required standard at this scale and is merely a way to prolong the use of fossil fuels.
Even more controversial than HyNet is the £5bn Peak Cluster project, also being heavily backed by the Government. This will see the building of a 125-mile CCS pipeline to carry CO2 from cement and lime producers in Derbyshire and Staffordshire.
Similar to HyNet, Peak Cluster will store the CO2 emissions under the Irish Sea. In Wirral there has been huge public opposition to the pipeline which campaigners claim will cause significant environmental damage to the peninsula’s rural landscape. However, this new platform is not part of Peak Cluster.
Installation of Douglas CCS forms part of a wider construction programme that is progressing across the entire Liverpool Bay CCS network, which is now approximately 50% complete.
Around 60% of the overall project expenditure from the investment is delivered through UK-based supply chains, supporting more than 2,000 jobs during construction and approximately 200 to 300 long-term roles over more than 25 years of operation.
Eni CCUS Holding is based in London and is owned jointly by Italian outfit Eni and Global Infrastructure Partners, part of BlackRock.— in Liverpool Bay.

The developer of a windfarm in Eday (Orkney) says it will be offering land for community use is one option being considered by GreenPower, which is looking into how islanders will benefit from its proposed Neven Point Wind Farm.
The Alloa-based renewable energy company provided the update as further information as been lodged with the local authority’s planning team. GreenPower is looking to build five turbines, up to 180 metres, near Greentoft.
Last year, interviews with a number of residents who had strong concerns about the Neven Point development, claiming it threatened the fabric of life in the island.
The planning application for the windfarm was submitted in June 2025. In the months since, dozens of objections have been lodged with Orkney Islands Council’s planning department.
Eday Community Council said in its submission last year that it is maintaining a neutral stance on whether the development should go ahead.
The Neven Point Wind Farm project is located on Greentoft Farm land on the southern edge of Eday and was initially mooted in 2018 as a 10- turbine proposal. 
Following initial feasibility work, the design was reduced to an 8-turbine proposal, and a Scoping Report setting out the proposed scope of environmental survey work was submitted to Orkney Islands Council in 2019.
Planning for the proposed wind farm was submitted in June 2025 and can be viewed on the Orkney Islands Council website under the application reference: 25/203/ТРРМАЈ. А number of clarifications and supporting documents were submitted in September 2026 at the request of Orkney Islands Council. These documents are available below and can also be accessed on the Orkney Islands Council website using the same application reference
£156,000 and £195,000 per year in community benefit for the operational lifetime of the project. The exact amount will depend on the total capacity of turbines installed.
To facilitate the wind farm's construction, we propose building a separate landing point adjacent to the existing pier. This ensures that the existing pier and ferry service will be able to operate as usual.
Planning for the proposed landing point (reference 25/302/PPMAJ), and a marine licence application (00011446), were both submitted in September 2025. The planning application can be viewed on the Orkney Islands Council website and the marine licence application can be accessed via the Marine.gov.scot website.
Should you have any questions or @quire any further information then please contact us

HAUNTING CLUES EMERGE KILLING TWO FISHERMEN
IN 7-YEAR FISHING BOAT MYSTERY AFTER WRECKAGE FOUND OFF ISLAND
THE FISHING BOAT SANK IN 2019 — KILLING TWO FISHERMEN
https://www.foxnews.com/.../haunting-clues-emerge-7-year...
By Andrea Margolis Fox News
Published October 12, 2026 8:00am EDT
An organization believes it has found the wreckage of a fishing boat that sank over seven years ago — potentially solving a mystery surrounding the deaths of two fishermen.
Green Oceans, a Rhode Island-based environmental organization, announced the discovery of what it believes is the F/V Mistress in the waters off Block Island in September.
The vessel sank Jan. 1, 2019, according to the organization.
Two fishermen died in the incident, and the U.S. Coast Guard searched for the vessel following the sinking but never located the wreckage.
The F/V Mistress was discovered approximately 92 feet underwater, just 50 feet from the base of a wind turbine at the Block Island Wind Farm, according to Green Oceans.
Green Oceans announced the discovery of what it believes is the F/V Mistress, a fishing boat that disappeared more than seven years ago. (Green Oceans)
The organization reported that "apparent human remains" were also found at the site.
Michael Lombardi, president of Green Oceans, told Fox News Digital his organization began searching for the vessel after receiving tips from two contractors who had previously worked near turbine No. 1 at the Block Island Wind Farm.
One contractor reported hearing rumors of underwater wreckage — while another claimed to have personally spotted wreckage while conducting survey work at the site.
Lombardi said he later reviewed the Coast Guard's original accident report and plotted GPS coordinates associated with distress calls and other key details, which pointed investigators toward the turbine.
"Once plotted on a map, it became obvious where the search area should be focused, and it coincided perfectly with turbine 1," Lombardi said.
The F/V Mistress, seen above, sank on Jan. 1, 2019 — prompting a Coast Guard search that failed to locate the vessel's wreckage. (Green Oceans)
When asked by Fox News Digital how confident he was that the wreck was the F/V Mistress, Lombardi replied, "100%."
He added, "The dive team studied images of the vessel prior to diving the site and were focused on finding key identifying features.
… One striking item was the net drum. It has several unique features."
Tim Diaz, who survived the sinking, confirmed that the net drum belonged to the Mistress, according to Lombardi.
Diaz built the equipment himself.
The mystery isn't over — and Lombardi said there is still some "uncertainty" about what happened in the vessel's final moments, though he said it was undoubtedly in distress.
The wreckage believed to belong to the F/V Mistress, seen above at right, was discovered just 50 feet from the base of an offshore wind turbine, shown at left. (Green Oceans)
"Based on the orientation of the wreckage on the bottom, there is reason to investigate whether an avoidance maneuver to starboard was made in an attempt to avoid a collision with the turbine," he said.
"With the hull full of water, this maneuver could have ultimately caused the vessel to roll and then sink."
Lombardi said he hopes federal authorities will reopen the investigation to determine whether the two fishermen who died remain within the wreckage or were swept out to sea and whether such a maneuver contributed to the sinking.
"The USCG and all agencies involved do tremendous work to protect mariners out on the water," Lombardi said, adding that he hopes the discovery will help answer lingering questions about the tragedy.
Green Oceans hopes federal authorities will reopen the investigation into the F/V Mistress following the discovery of suspected wreckage near an offshore wind turbine. (Green Oceans)
As Green Oceans focuses on the environmental and maritime safety impacts of offshore wind development, Lombardi said the discovery could have implications for future permitting decisions.
"Had this accident been fully investigated in 2019, while having the vessel wreckage, the offshore wind permitting landscape would have been quite different with regard to safety considerations along the continental shelf," he said.

Eastern Green Link 1 (EGL1), a joint venture between National Grid Electricity Transmission and SP Transmission, part of SP Energy Networks, will see the creation of a 525kV, 2GW HVDC subsea transmission cable from Torness in East Lothian, Scotland to Hawthorn Pit in County Durham, England, enabling the transmission of renewable green energy to power more than two million homes.
EGL1 reached another significant milestone in the development of a new subsea electricity superhighway by awarding the Prysmian Group a £750m contract to deliver the UK's first 525kV HVDC electricity transmission cable. 
GE Vernova's Grid Solutions business and MYTILINEOS Energy & Metals have also been awarded a £1bn contract to supply and construct two HVDC converter stations, one at each end of the link.
The UK is transforming the electricity grid - the largest overhaul in generations to help deliver a cleaner, greener and more secure energy system for the future. This means multi-billion investments in new electricity transmission projects across the country.
This upgrade, which will help move more clean energy from where it is generated to where it is needed and play a major role in the UK moving towards its net zero target, includes six subsea links between Scotland and England of which this joint project is the first.— at Torness.

This was one of the images accompanying one of our posts about the renewed threat to Barningham Moor in County Durham, this time by Fred Olsen - the Hope Moor wind farm.  
The lady referred to is the late MaryElizabeth Mann, as she was known to all her many anti-industrial wind campaigner friends across the UK (no solar, BESS or any of the other infrastructure threats in the days, nearly 30 years ago, when she took up her sword and fought - although had there been, we are sure that she'd have fought as valiantly now as then.)
The sword has been picked up by many, including Shane Oxer and Suzy Wilson who are known to our page.  Lord Botham (Sir Ian Botham) and Alan Hinkes, the accomplished mountaineer, have joined the voices trying to protect moorland and yesterday, a walk took place across the moor.
Shane has written about it - 'Hope Moor: The Day People Stood on the Land and Said No'.
'Mary Mann carried the old fight. Lord Botham has helped give the new fight a national voice. The people who gathered on the moor showed that the spirit of resistance is alive on the land itself.
For Barningham. For Hope Moor. For the views across the Pennines and beyond  For the North. For England’s living landscape.
Stand up. Speak out. Defend the moors.
Because the land remembers — and so must we.'
We believe that our late friend MaryElizabeth would have cheered the walkers on and been so proud of them.

Oral evidence in Parliament: Secretary of State Miatta Fahnbulleh faces ESNZ questions on the energy transition, energy resilience, energy bills and more
On Wednesday 14th October the Energy Security and Net Zero Committee will question new Secretary of State for Energy Security and Net Zero Miatta Fahnbulleh for the first time.
The session comes at a critical moment in the UK’s energy transition, as energy costs once again rising under pressure from geopolitical events continue to drive a national affordability crisis.
Just before Party conferences the Committee published a report on building UK public support for the energy transition, and is also expected shortly to make its final report on the cost of energy in the UK.
Areas of questioning to the Secretary of State and Permanent Secretary will likely include:
Support for the energy transition among the UK public
The costs and complexity of building out a renewable-ready national grid and storage capacity
Historically high energy prices and Government plans for relief
Risks to energy infrastructure in the new geopolitical reality and Government defences against them
UK priorities and action at COP 31 in November

RAPID  - Rushing Approval, Prioritising Infrastructure Delivery (WEA's acronym)
RAPID  - The Routing and Planning through Interoperable Data (SSEN's acronym)
We already have SSEN attempting to rule the Northern half of the Scottish roost by leaning on Reporters to rush through the OHLs and associated infrastructure.
A reminder here of one example;  what Paul Reid, SSEN's KC said at the Beauly-Peterhead OHL Ornithology hearing:
The applicant would take any delay to that timetable very seriously and accordingly I should make clear that should the timetable be departed from, the applicant will request full written reasons for that, along with, and in addition to, the reasons which have already ben requested and which remain awaited for the agricultural decision.
What we said in one of the paragraphs of the summary of the close of the B-P OHL hearing, on Conditions:
Rosie Leven then ran through the timetable. When she'd finished, PR complained about the time frame. Rosie Leven so nicely put him in his place - and the matter into perspective - by saying that additional information meant that the timescale envisaged might not be met but they were very much trying to ensure that the overall timescale is met.
Then we've got the last part of SSEN's disgraceful e mail of 22 September to Rhoda Banfro, The Highland Council solicitor who had asked for four extra days for the Council's closing submission to be presented:
For the avoidance of doubt, the Applicant expects Reporters to adhere to the 3 December date for submitting their Report.
And, finally, we have all the e mails from the planning consultant Ian Kelly to the DPEA referring to the haste at which the infrastructure PLIs are being conducted.
This is part of just one:
The public perception in respect of these cases is already poor as a totally unseemly and unjustified haste is applied to the cases, largely to satisfy the time requirements of SSEN (there being no statutory requirements), and in the circumstances where the objectors, but seemingly nobody else, can see that there is absolutely no up to date justification of any sort for the expenditure of billions of pounds of bill payers' monies on infrastructure for which there is no need.
So, that's the background to why we say that SSEN are attempting to push the Reporters forward.
And now we have RAPID, announced by SSEN last week.  a joint initiative to accelerate grid development from around five years to two. The initiative has secured more than £450,000 from Ofgem's Strategic Innovation Fund to move into its next development phase.
SSEN Transmission is leading the initiative, and it brings together SPEN Transmission,  National Grid Electricity Transmission, NESO and Arup.
The next phase will run for six months and develop a common digital framework connecting engineering, planning, consenting and land information.
RAPID brings together transmission network operators, the system operator and industry partners to tackle a challenge we all share. By developing a more consistent approach to how data is structured, shared and used, we believe there is a real opportunity to significantly speed up the development of the infrastructure needed to unlock new clean energy projects. Brant Wilson, Senior Manager of Innovation at SSEN Transmission
Wait a wee minute!  If NESO is still developing its strategic picture of what is needed and where, as follows, how do we ensure that the drive to accelerate infrastructure delivery remains aligned with that evolving picture? 
SSEP - Strategic Spatial Energy Plan -  where generation and storage should be located across Great Britain.
Autumn 2027 for the final plan. Draft plan and environmental report consultation expected in early 2027. 
RESP - Regional Energy Strategic Plan - what energy system Scotland and each other region will need, taking a whole-system view. 
2028 for the first full plans. The transitional RESP (tRESP) was published on 30January 2026. The final RESP methodology is now due by the end of 2026, subject to approval. 
CSNP - Centralised Strategic Network Plan - what networks are needed to transport energy around Great Britain, including electricity, gas and hydrogen. 15 December 2028 for the first published plan. Ofgem has formally revised the timetable to align with the delayed SSEP
We say:
SSEN has much to say about development and delivery, but where, in this account, are the communities who will live with the infrastructure?
https://www.ssen-transmission.co.uk/.../industry-wide.../

We're reprising our image of five days ago which introduced the post and link that the Dogger Bank project was seeking a third exemption from the transmission licensing rules. 
The Times had a piece yesterday about delays to CfD take-up, starting with Dogger Bank, but going on to cover Seagreen (which Kathryn Porter and other energy experts have covered repeatedly).
SSE gets a special mention:
The ability to delay contract start dates was designed to accommodate commissioning problems such as those seen at Dogger Bank A. But SSE is among developers who have also controversially delayed contract start dates purely to cash in on higher market prices. 
We have so much in the archives about gaming of the system, delays to CfD start dates being just one.  And who suffers?  Consumers who are forced to pay market prices and not the contracted CfD ones.
From 2017 - a joint paper by Professor Gordon Hughes, Dr John Constable and Dr Capell Aris:
We introduced it thus:
Prof Gordon Hughes and Drs Capell Aris and John Constable, in a report for GWPF, pull out the teeth of the weasels and their other sock puppets - the gormless media - and the pollie parrots - one by one and without anaesthetic - because of the false hysteria and misinformation which has surrounded the offshore strike prices.
We've put a link to that report at the end.  It ended  with:
Contrary to media exaggerations, the low CfD prices are commercial speculation, not the dawn of a new age for offshore wind and renewables.
The Government did close the 'delay' loophole in 2023, but any project awarded a CfD before then can just carry on.  
In September, we had yet another post on gaming of the system.  David Turver was quoted:
The ability to delay the start of CfDs was originally intended to help developers manage the risk of construction delays.
But in some cases, the wind farms have been built already and they are simply choosing not to activate the contracts so they can get higher merchant power prices. 
And that same piece quoted an energy executive as saying that developers are 'making out like bandits' - an expression first used, we believe, by Matt Ridley and John Constable in 2017.
https://www.thetimes.com/business/companies-markets/article/dogger-wind-farm-north-sea-energy-dwcnsltqd?utm_source=Sailthru&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=Daily%20Briefing%20-%20Monday%20October%2012th%202026&utm_term=audience_DAILY_BRIEFING
'The world’s largest offshore wind farm is struggling with serious construction problems that threaten to further delay promised cheap power for consumers.
The Dogger Bank project in the North Sea got the go-ahead in 2019 with a contract locking in a record-low price for the electricity it would generate for 15 years.
More than 80 miles off the coast of Yorkshire, it was originally scheduled to start delivering cheap power as early as 2023 but has repeatedly delayed its contract start dates after the failure of two turbine blades triggered “cascading” problems. 
It is still grappling with “unforeseen and significant technical issues with the installation, remediation and commissioning of wind turbines”, according to a government document.
Dogger Bank is due to comprise 277 turbines with a total capacity of 3.6 gigawatts, expected to generate enough clean energy to power the equivalent of six million homes. It is co-owned by SSE, the FTSE 100 energy group, Equinor, the Norwegian state oil and gas group, and the offshore wind company Vargronn of Norway. 
The wind farm is being built in three stages. Dogger Bank A has a contract priced at £55.01 per megawatt-hour (MWh) today, which would be cheaper than any operational UK offshore wind farm, and roughly a third of wholesale market prices, which have risen to £162.50/MWh. Dogger Bank B and C have contracts at £57.92/MWh.
When the project was approved the government said it would mean renewables generating “below market prices and without additional subsidy on bills” for the first time. 
However, it is not clear when this promised cheap power will now materialise.
Although Dogger Bank A generated electricity from its first turbine in 2023 it suffered a big setback the following year with two separate blade failures that forced it to slow construction work. It is still suffering “continuing knock-on impacts from the 2024 blade failure events and subsequent remediation programme”, including “ongoing technical defects and resource constraints”, according to the government document published last week.
Power that is being generated during the commissioning period continues to be sold at high prevailing market prices.
The first chunk of Dogger Bank A is required to activate its fixed-price contract by November 30 or risk contract cancellation, but it is not clear whether the project will meet required conditions to do so. It is unlikely to be in the government’s interest to cancel the contract, however, given the desire for cheap power to cut soaring energy bills. 
The entire Dogger Bank wind farm is scheduled to be supplying power at its guaranteed prices by the middle of next year, but developers could exercise the right to delay the contract start dates for some of the subsequent phases to as late as 2029 without risking cancellation.
The ability to delay contract start dates was designed to accommodate commissioning problems such as those seen at Dogger Bank A. But SSE is among developers who have also controversially delayed contract start dates purely to cash in on higher market prices. 
Its Seagreen wind farm, off the Angus coast in Scotland, which also has a contract priced at £57.92/MWh, was fully operational in October 2023 yet has repeatedly opted to delay its contract start date. Promised cheap power from that project is now not expected until at least the end of March and could yet be delayed further. 
A spokesperson for Dogger Bank Wind Farm said: “While some construction delays have previously been reported on Dogger Bank A, we’re maintaining commissioning momentum. We expect the project to be substantially all available for generation by the end of 2026, with final commissioning work continuing into 2027. As a project of unprecedented scale, Dogger Bank A will be a world-class asset once fully operational, providing much-needed secure and affordable energy for Britain.”
Hughes/Constable/Aris

Last month CX Tech Limited submitted a proposal to build eight 120MW data centres on land north of the decommissioned nuclear power station at Chapelcross.
The campus would have a total capacity of 1000MW, and if approved, would be larger than any data centre campus currently in operation across the globe, with the biggest currently being Switch’s Citadel Campus in Nevada, in the US, which has a capacity of 650MW.
Local campaigners have already voiced their concerns over the plans, arguing that it will be built on farmland rather than the existing Chapelcross brownfield site while covering a total area the size of 77 football pitches.
There have also been concerns raised over the proposed energy usage at the site, as at full capacity it would use roughly the same amount of electricity as 2.2 million homes.
However, despite hundreds of complaints online, and more than 5000 people lodging objections to the proposal via a portal created by the Scottish Greens in less than a week, the application on the council’s website shows zero comments made.
A spokesperson for Dumfries and Galloway told The National that due to the “significant volume” of comments made to the local authority, it won’t post any of them online until the end of the notification period.
